preamble: Raising the open nucleus of [ai] to mid [e] gives [ei], the glide pulling the first element upward. The Proto-Germanic diphthong *ai became ei in Old Norse and, outside a few consonantal environments, in Old High German. In Galician-Portuguese a Vulgar Latin [ai] created by metathesis of yod (-ārius > *-airu) became ei, giving the productive suffix -eiro. In Czech, tautosyllabic aj became ej in the Humanistic period (vajce > vejce 'egg', daj > dej 'give!'), while heterosyllabic aj stayed (vajec 'of eggs', dají 'they will give'). Common Czech ej for Old Czech ý (malej 'small', bejt 'to be') also has a recorded aj stage: Wiktionary gives the 15th-century pronunciation of malý as /ˈmaliː/ or /ˈmalaj/, and Czech Wikipedia (Diftongizace) says the diphthong was first written ay. No cited source dates this aj together with the old aj, so malej and bejt are not listed as examples.

examples.note: Proto-Germanic *ai became ei; Old English stān and Gothic stains show other outcomes.
Before r, w, h and word-finally *ai monophthongized to ē instead (e.g. OHG rēho 'roe deer').
Metathesis of i in -ārius produced [ai], which was raised to ei; Spanish carried the change on to -ero.
Only tautosyllabic aj changed; the genitive plural vajec, with a and j in different syllables, keeps aj (Wikipedia, History of the Czech language).

examples.from: Old Czech daj 'give!' (2nd sg. imperative of dáti)
examples.note: Wikipedia's example; dají 'they will give' keeps heterosyllabic aj.
